rows.stem: Cistron is a segment of DNA coding for a :
rows.solution: A **cistron** is the segment of DNA that codes for a **polypeptide**. NCERT defines the structural gene in a transcription unit this way: in eukaryotes the structural genes are mostly **monocistronic** (one cistron, one polypeptide), while in bacteria they are usually **polycistronic** (several cistrons, each coding for a separate polypeptide, transcribed together). The mRNA is only the intermediate that carries the coded message, and tRNA and rRNA are not polypeptides. So the answer is option (A) Polypeptide only.

rows.stem: In a pedigree chart, if two unaffected individuals have a child with the trait, what is the most likely mode of inheritance for this trait ?
rows.solution:
If two **unaffected** parents have an **affected** child, the trait must be **recessive**: each parent carries the allele hidden in the heterozygous condition and passes it on, so the child receives two copies. A dominant trait cannot appear this way, because a dominant allele would have shown in at least one of the parents.
- An autosomal recessive trait can appear in a son or a daughter of two carrier parents, in about one child in four.
- An X-linked recessive trait could explain an affected son of a carrier mother, but an affected daughter would need an affected father, which the parents here are not.

So the most likely mode is autosomal recessive (as in sickle-cell anaemia or phenylketonuria). So the answer is option (B) Autosomal recessive.

rows.stem: If a natural population with 200 individuals is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for a gene with two alleles A and a, with the gene frequency of allele A of \(0{\cdot}8\), the genotype frequency of Aa will be :
rows.solution:
In Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium the allele frequencies satisfy \(p + q = 1\) and the genotype frequencies are \(p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1\), where \(2pq\) is the frequency of the heterozygote Aa.
- Frequency of A: \(p = 0{\cdot}8\), so the frequency of a is \(q = 1 - 0{\cdot}8 = 0{\cdot}2\).
- Frequency of Aa \(= 2pq = 2 \times 0{\cdot}8 \times 0{\cdot}2 = 0{\cdot}32\).

The population size of 200 does not enter the frequency; it would only give the number of heterozygotes, \(0{\cdot}32 \times 200 = 64\). So the answer is option (C) \(0{\cdot}32\).

rows.stem:
Select the statements that are true for a typical monocotyledonous embryo from the given options.
(i) Scutellum is present towards the centre of the embryonal axis.
(ii) Embryonal axis of the lower end has radicle and root cap covered by coleoptile.
(iii) The portion of embryonal axis above the level of attachment of scutellum is epicotyl.
(iv) Shoot apex and few leaf primordia of embryo are enclosed in a hollow foliar structure.
Choose the correct answer from the following :
rows.solution:
Checking each statement against the structure of a monocot (grass) embryo described in NCERT:
- (i) is false: the single cotyledon, the **scutellum**, is situated towards **one side (lateral)** of the embryonal axis, not at its centre.
- (ii) is false: at its lower end the embryonal axis has the radicle and root cap enclosed in an undifferentiated sheath called the **coleorhiza**, not the coleoptile.
- (iii) is true: the portion of the embryonal axis above the level of attachment of the scutellum is the **epicotyl**.
- (iv) is true: the epicotyl has a **shoot apex and a few leaf primordia enclosed in a hollow foliar structure**, the **coleoptile**.

So the true statements are (iii) and (iv). So the answer is option (C) (iii) and (iv).

rows.stem:
Given below are a few statements with reference to the human sperm.
(i) Sperm head contains a large nucleus and a lot of cytoplasm.
(ii) Mitochondria in the middle piece of a sperm provides ATP for the sperm motility.
(iii) Posterior part of the sperm head is covered by acrosome.
(iv) Spermatids undergo maturation into spermatozoa by the process of spermiogenesis.
(v) Acrosomal secretions help in the entry of the sperm into the ovum at the time of fertilization.
Choose the option with all true statements from the given options :
rows.solution:
Checking each statement against the structure of a human sperm:
- (i) is false: the sperm head contains an elongated haploid **nucleus** with very little cytoplasm; a lot of cytoplasm would only slow the sperm down.
- (ii) is true: the middle piece has numerous **mitochondria**, which produce the energy (ATP) for the movement of the tail that gives the sperm its motility.
- (iii) is false: the **anterior** portion of the sperm head is covered by a cap-like structure, the **acrosome**.
- (iv) is true: spermatids are transformed into spermatozoa (sperms) by the process called **spermiogenesis**.
- (v) is true: the acrosome is filled with enzymes that help the sperm enter the ovum at fertilisation.

So the true statements are (ii), (iv) and (v). So the answer is option (C) (ii), (iv) and (v).

rows.stem:
A normal couple produces half the sons as haemophilic and half the daughters as carriers.
Choose the option that correctly indicates the chromosome on which the gene for this trait is located.

options.label: D
options.text: Both the X-chromosomes of the mother

rows.solution:
Haemophilia is a **sex-linked recessive** disorder: its gene lies on the X chromosome, and the Y chromosome carries no allele for it. Writing the normal allele on X as X and the haemophilia allele as \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\):
- The father is normal, so he is XY.
- For half the sons to be haemophilic, the mother must carry the allele while being normal herself, so she is a carrier, \(\text{X}\text{X}^{\text{h}}\).
- Sons get their X from the mother and the Y from the father: half are XY (normal) and half are \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\text{Y}\) (haemophilic).
- Daughters get the father's normal X and one of the mother's X chromosomes: half are XX (normal) and half are \(\text{X}\text{X}^{\text{h}}\) (carriers).

The father cannot be the source, since he passes his X only to daughters and his Y (which has no such gene) to sons, and a mother with the allele on both X chromosomes would be haemophilic herself and would make every son affected. So the gene lies on one X chromosome of the mother. So the answer is option (C) One X-chromosome of mother.

rows.stem: If the sequence of bases in DNA is ATTCGATG, then the sequence of bases in the transcript will be :
rows.solution:
During transcription the RNA is built on the **template strand** of DNA by complementary base pairing, with **uracil (U) in place of thymine**: A pairs with U, T with A, G with C and C with G. Taking the given strand ATTCGATG as the template, as the marking scheme does, and writing the complementary base under each base in turn:
- A \(\rightarrow\) U, T \(\rightarrow\) A, T \(\rightarrow\) A, C \(\rightarrow\) G, G \(\rightarrow\) C, A \(\rightarrow\) U, T \(\rightarrow\) A, G \(\rightarrow\) C.

This gives the transcript UAAGCUAC. (Had the given strand been the coding strand instead, the transcript would have the same sequence with U for T, that is AUUCGAUG; the stem does not say which strand is given, and the key treats it as the template.) So the answer is option (B) UAAGCUAC.

rows.stem: In a translational unit UTRs are present at :

options.label: A
options.text: 5' end (after start codon) and 3' end (after stop codon).

options.label: B
options.text: 5' end (before start codon) and 3' end (before stop codon).

options.label: C
options.text: 5' end (after start codon) and 3' end (before stop codon).

options.label: D
options.text: 5' end (before start codon) and 3' end (after stop codon).

rows.solution:
An mRNA carries additional sequences that are **not translated**, the **untranslated regions (UTRs)**. They are present at both ends of the translational unit:
- the **5'-UTR** lies at the 5' end, **before the start codon** (AUG);
- the **3'-UTR** lies at the 3' end, **after the stop codon**.

The UTRs are required for an efficient translation process. So the answer is option (D) 5' end (before start codon) and 3' end (after stop codon).

rows.stem: The lymphoid organ located within the lining of respiratory, digestive and urinogenital tract is :
rows.solution: Lymphoid tissue is also located within the lining of the major tracts (respiratory, digestive and urogenital), and is called **mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT)**. It constitutes about **50 per cent** of the lymphoid tissue in the human body. The other choices are not lymphoid organs at all: GEAC is the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, NACO the National AIDS Control Organisation and RCH the Reproductive and Child Health care programme. So the answer is option (B) MALT.

rows.stem: Land reptiles which went back into water about 200 mya to evolve into fish-like reptiles were :
rows.solution: In the history of life on earth, some of the land reptiles went back into water, about **200 million years ago**, to evolve into **fish-like reptiles**, the **Ichthyosaurs** (Ichthyosaurus). Tyrannosaurus, Stegosaurus and Brachiosaurus were land dinosaurs; Tyrannosaurus rex, the biggest of them, was about 20 feet in height. So the answer is option (A) Ichthyosaurus.

rows.stem: Certain viruses used as biological control agents belong to the genus :
rows.solution: **Baculoviruses** are pathogens that attack insects and other arthropods, and the majority of those used as **biological control agents** belong to the genus **Nucleopolyhedrovirus**. They are excellent candidates for species-specific, narrow-spectrum insecticidal applications: they have no negative impact on plants, mammals, birds, fish or even non-target insects, which makes them especially useful in integrated pest management, for example where an ecologically sensitive area is being treated. So the answer is option (A) Nucleopolyhedrovirus.

rows.stem: The cloning site present in the ampicillin resistance gene of E. coli cloning vector pBR322 is :

Assertion (A) : An antibody is a protein molecule made by the lymphocytes.
Reason (R) : An antibody binds to a specific foreign antigen and neutralizes its odd effects.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: antibodies are **proteins** (immunoglobulins), each made of four peptide chains, two small light chains and two longer heavy chains (\(\text{H}_2\text{L}_2\)). They are produced by the **B-lymphocytes**, which release an army of antibodies into the blood in response to pathogens; this is the humoral immune response. The Reason is also true: each antibody binds specifically to the foreign antigen that elicited it and neutralises it, which is how the B-lymphocytes fight the pathogen. The marking scheme takes the Reason as the explanation of why the lymphocytes make these protein molecules, although strictly the Reason describes what an antibody does rather than why it is a protein made by lymphocytes. So both statements are true and the Reason is taken as the correct explanation of the Assertion, which is option (A).

rows.stem:
Answer the following questions with respect to the sex determining mechanism observed in honey bee.
(a) What is the type of cell division involved in the formation of gametes in a female bee and a male bee respectively ?
(b) Name the type of sex determination system observed in honey bee.
(c) What is the sex of honey bee formed from the unfertilised eggs ? Write the number of chromosomes present in it.
rows.solution:
(a) Gamete formation in honey bees:
- The **female** bee (queen) is **diploid** (32 chromosomes), so she forms her eggs by **meiosis**.
- The **male** bee (drone) is **haploid** (16 chromosomes), so he forms his sperms by **mitosis**.

(b) Honey bees show the **haplo-diploid** sex determination system: the sex of an offspring depends on the number of sets of chromosomes it receives.

(c) An unfertilised egg develops by **parthenogenesis** into a **male** (drone). It has **16** chromosomes, a single (haploid) set. A fertilised egg, with 32 chromosomes, develops into a female (a queen or a worker).

rows.stem:
(i) Explain how human pro-insulin is processed in the cell to become a fully mature functional insulin.
(ii) Describe how human insulin is produced using the techniques of genetic engineering.
rows.solution:
(i) Insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains, **chain A** and **chain B**, linked together by **disulphide bridges**.
- In mammals, including humans, insulin is synthesised as a **pro-hormone**, the **pro-insulin**, which, like a pro-enzyme, must be processed before it becomes fully mature and functional.
- Pro-insulin contains an **extra stretch** called the **C-peptide** (connecting peptide) joining the A and B chains.
- During maturation into insulin, the **C-peptide is removed**, leaving the A and B chains held together by the disulphide bonds as functional insulin.

(ii) Producing human insulin by genetic engineering (Eli Lilly, an American company, 1983):
- Two DNA sequences corresponding to the **A and B chains** of human insulin were prepared.
- These were introduced into **plasmids of E. coli** to produce the insulin chains.
- The chains **A and B were produced separately**, extracted, and combined by creating **disulphide bonds** to form human insulin.

This avoids the main difficulty in producing insulin by recombinant DNA technology, getting it assembled into a mature form, and it gives insulin that does not cause the allergy or immune reactions that insulin taken from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs could cause in some patients.

rows.stem:
(i) Explain the working of a simple stirred-tank bioreactor.
(ii) Describe what is meant by downstream processing.
rows.solution:
(i) A bioreactor provides the optimal conditions (temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins, oxygen) for growing large volumes of culture and obtaining the desired product. A **simple stirred-tank bioreactor** works as follows:
- It is usually **cylindrical or has a curved base**, which facilitates the mixing of the reactor contents.
- A **stirrer** (motor-driven, with flat-bladed impellers) facilitates **even mixing and oxygen availability** throughout the bioreactor.
- Alternatively, **sterile air can be bubbled** through the reactor.
- It has an **agitator system**, an **oxygen delivery system** and a **foam control system** (a foam breaker).
- It has a **temperature control system** and a **pH control system** (acid or base added for pH control).
- It has **sampling ports**, so that small volumes of the culture can be withdrawn periodically, and an inlet for steam for sterilisation.

The working can also be shown as a labelled diagram: a cylindrical vessel holding the culture broth, a motor on top driving a shaft with flat-bladed impellers, a foam breaker near the top, an inlet for acid or base for pH control, a steam inlet for sterilisation and a sterile air inlet at the base.

(ii) After the biosynthetic stage in the bioreactor, the product has to undergo a series of processes before it is ready for marketing as a finished product. These processes include **separation and purification**, which are collectively referred to as **downstream processing**.
- The product is formulated with suitable **preservatives**.
- Such a formulation has to undergo thorough **clinical trials**, as in the case of drugs.
- Strict **quality control testing** is required for each product, and the downstream processing and quality control vary from product to product.
